title: The Identity That Erases the Partition Function

body:
An unnormalised density is almost never what we want. Energy-based models, product-of-experts, exponential families with intractable base measures, almost every probabilistic model written down with an $\exp$ and no apology, all come with a shadow — the partition function

$$ Z(\theta) = \int \exp(-E_\theta(x))\,dx $$

that we need to compute to turn an energy into a probability. $Z$ is the reason maximum likelihood is expensive for these models; it is the reason MCMC and noise-contrastive estimation exist. But there is an older route that walks past the problem rather than attacking it. It uses a single identity from Stein's 1972 work on normal approximation and a 2005 paper by Hyvärinen that noticed it would also work for parameter estimation. That identity is the backbone of score matching, and through score matching, of every modern diffusion model. The trick, stripped of context, is to rewrite a thing you cannot compute as a thing you can.

## Why this matters now

Diffusion models have made score estimation the central training objective of generative modelling. Training a neural network to approximate $\nabla_x \log p(x)$ is, these days, the most common workload in the field, measured in GPU-years. Almost everyone who writes a diffusion loss writes a denoising score matching objective without thinking about where it comes from. The derivation is instructive in its own right: the same two lines of calculation are what let score matching train an energy-based model without ever touching $Z$, let denoising score matching train a diffusion model without an explicit likelihood, and let sliced score matching scale either to high-dimensional data. The identity is one short argument used three ways.

It is also a case study in how a trick from one field can quietly become infrastructure in another. Stein's original motivation was a Berry–Esseen-style bound on normal approximation for sums of dependent variables; parameter estimation for unnormalised models was not on his map. Hyvärinen's 2005 paper is a modest-looking JMLR note that noticed the same calculation turns an intractable likelihood problem into a tractable one. Fifteen years later it became the training rule for the most expensive models anyone has trained. The underlying observation is very small, and the line of derivation can be reconstructed from scratch in under a page, which is what the rest of this post does.

## The identity

Fix a smooth density $p$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with gradient of log-density $\nabla \log p(x)$, called the score $s(x)$. Under mild regularity — $p$ differentiable, $f$ differentiable, and the boundary term $p(x) f(x) \to 0$ as $\|x\| \to \infty$ — integration by parts yields

$$ \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\, f(X)\, s(X) + f'(X) \,\right] \;=\; 0. $$

In one dimension the computation is just

$$ \int p(x)\, f(x)\, \frac{p'(x)}{p(x)}\, dx \;=\; \int f(x)\, p'(x)\, dx \;=\; \big[f p\big]_{-\infty}^{\infty} - \int f'(x)\, p(x)\, dx. $$

For $f = \mathrm{id}$ and $p$ Gaussian this is Stein's original lemma; the general version, with $f$ ranging over a test class, is Charles Stein's identity (Stein 1972). Its content is that the score of $p$ is determined, in a weak sense, by the operator $f \mapsto \mathbb{E}_p[f'(X)]$ — something you can estimate from samples without knowing $p$.

## Score matching

Hyvärinen (2005) asked what happens if the test function is itself a parametric model's score. Call the model's score $s_\theta$ and define

$$ J(\theta) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\, \| s_\theta(X) - s(X) \|^2 \,\right]. $$

This is the loss we would like to minimise, but it depends on $s(X) = \nabla \log p(X)$, which we do not have. Expand the square:

$$ J(\theta) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\| s_\theta(X) \|^2\right] - \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[s_\theta(X)^\top s(X)\right] + \text{const}. $$

Apply the identity component by component to the middle term, with $f = s_\theta^{i}$ in the $i$-th coordinate, and the cross term becomes $-\mathbb{E}_p[\mathrm{tr}(\nabla s_\theta(X))]$. Collect terms:

$$ \tilde{J}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\, \tfrac{1}{2}\, \| s_\theta(X) \|^2 \;+\; \mathrm{tr}\!\left( \nabla s_\theta(X) \right) \,\right] \;+\; \text{const}. $$

Both terms are quantities of the model only, averaged over samples from $p$. The data's score $s(X)$ has vanished. Where did $Z$ go? For an energy-based model $p_\theta(x) = \exp(-E_\theta(x))/Z(\theta)$, the model's score is $s_\theta(x) = -\nabla_x E_\theta(x)$: the $\log Z(\theta)$ term has no $x$-gradient, so $Z$ never appears in $s_\theta$ nor in $\tilde J$. Hyvärinen's observation is that once you only need gradients with respect to $x$, the partition function is already gone.

## From a theorem to a training loop

Hyvärinen's $\tilde J$ is honest but inconvenient. Computing $\mathrm{tr}(\nabla s_\theta(x))$ in $d$ dimensions requires $d$ backward passes, one per diagonal entry. On images that is a non-starter. Two reformulations saved the technique.

Denoising score matching (Vincent 2011) replaces $p$ with a slightly smoothed version. Let $q_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\tilde x; x, \sigma^2 I)$ and $p_\sigma(\tilde x) = \int p(x)\, q_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x)\, dx$. Vincent's identity, again one integration by parts, is

$$ \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_{p_\sigma}\!\left[ \| s_\theta(\tilde X) - \nabla \log p_\sigma(\tilde X) \|^2 \right] \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_{p(x) q_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x)}\!\left[ \| s_\theta(\tilde X) - \nabla_{\tilde x} \log q_\sigma(\tilde X \mid X) \|^2 \right] + \text{const}, $$

and because $\nabla_{\tilde x} \log q_\sigma(\tilde x \mid x) = (x - \tilde x)/\sigma^2$, the right-hand side is a loss on a known target. In code the training step is: draw a sample $x$, perturb it to $\tilde x = x + \sigma \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, and regress $s_\theta(\tilde x, \sigma)$ onto $-\varepsilon/\sigma$. That is exactly the training loss of modern diffusion models at a single noise level. Song and Ermon (2019) extended this across a schedule of $\sigma$'s — one network, many noise levels — and got the first competitive score-based generative model on images.

Sliced score matching (Song, Garg, Shi and Ermon, UAI 2019) attacks the trace directly. Hutchinson's identity says $\mathrm{tr}(A) = \mathbb{E}_v[v^\top A v]$ for $v$ with zero mean and identity covariance. Applying this to the Jacobian $\nabla s_\theta(x)$ turns the $d$ backward passes into one Jacobian-vector product. Both techniques take Hyvärinen's theorem and make it operational on high-dimensional data.

## A tiny experiment

Here is a 20-line sanity check: fit a 1D Gaussian with score matching and watch $Z$ disappear.

```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(10000) * 2.0 + 1.5        # true N(1.5, 2^2)

mu    = torch.tensor(0.0, requires_grad=True)
log_s = torch.tensor(0.0, requires_grad=True)
opt   = torch.optim.Adam([mu, log_s], lr=5e-2)

for _ in range(2000):
    s = torch.exp(log_s)
    score   = -(x - mu) / s**2             # d/dx log N(x; mu, s^2)
    d_score = -1.0 / s**2                  # d/dx of the score
    loss = (0.5 * score**2 + d_score).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

print(mu.item(), torch.exp(log_s).item())  # ~ 1.5, 2.0
```

No normalisation constant is computed. No likelihood is written. The gradient signal comes entirely from the two terms Hyvärinen's identity produced. Recovering $(\mu, \sigma)$ on a Gaussian is not impressive in itself; the point is that the loss would work identically if we replaced $-(x - \mu)/\sigma^2$ by a neural network $s_\theta(x)$ and let the trace term — or its Hutchinson estimate — regularise against degenerate solutions.

## What it buys you in practice

Reach for score matching whenever the normalising constant of your model is painful. That covers more ground than it first seems. Any model written as $\exp(-E_\theta(x))/Z$ with $E_\theta$ a neural net is an energy-based model, including implicit learned priors for inverse problems and the drift fields used in continuous-time generative models. If you are already using diffusion models, the loss you are writing is denoising score matching and inherits its asymptotic consistency. If you are training something whose log-likelihood is only tractable up to a constant — a spin system, a product of experts, a conditional energy over a structured output — score matching gives a consistent estimator you can run on samples, no MCMC in the inner loop. The practical cost is estimator variance on high-dimensional scores and, for the Hyvärinen form, the $d$ backward passes in the trace; both are handled by the denoising or sliced variants.

A second habit the identity should install is noticing when a derivation is secretly an integration by parts. The move from the matching objective $J$ to the operational $\tilde J$ is the same move that defines Fisher's information as either $\mathbb{E}[(\nabla \log p)^2]$ or $-\mathbb{E}[\nabla^2 \log p]$, and the same move that turns a reparameterised expectation into a score-function estimator in reinforcement learning. In each case, the trick shifts a derivative off something you cannot differentiate (the data's density, a non-differentiable sampler) onto something you can (the model's score, the log-probability of an action). Score matching is the version of that trick that pays off when the thing you cannot differentiate is $\log Z$.

## Limits and open questions

The identity has conditions, and they matter. The boundary term $[s_\theta\, p]_{-\infty}^{\infty}$ must vanish, which rules out models whose tails are heavier than the data's; a Gaussian-tailed score network against a Cauchy data distribution does not satisfy the hypothesis, and the estimator is not even unbiased. Score matching is a second-moment method and so, like least squares, is sensitive to outliers; robust alternatives based on diffusion kernels or $\alpha$-divergences exist but are less standard. On multi-modal data at a single noise level, the score estimate is poor in the low-density regions between modes — the exact failure that motivated Song and Ermon's multi-scale training. More fundamentally, the identity is silent about discrete data. Extensions to discrete score matching via categorical scores or Fisher divergences are an active area; the elegant proof we used here breaks because integration by parts is replaced by a summation by parts whose boundary terms are not free. The Song and Kingma (2021) tutorial surveys where the technique now lives and where it does not yet reach.

## Further reading

- Charles Stein, *A bound for the error in the normal approximation to the distribution of a sum of dependent random variables*, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability, Vol. 2 (1972), 583–602. <https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bsmsp/1200514239>. The paper that introduced Stein's method; the lemma we used is in section 2.
- Aapo Hyvärinen, *Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching*, JMLR 6 (2005), 695–709. <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v6/hyvarinen05a.html>. The source for the score matching identity $\tilde J$; the proofs and the natural-image ICA application are worth reading in full.
- Pascal Vincent, *A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders*, Neural Computation 23(7) (2011), 1661–1674. <https://doi.org/10.1162/NECO_a_00142>. The denoising score matching derivation; the Parzen-density view makes the Gaussian noise target obvious once you see it.
- Yang Song, Sahaj Garg, Jiaxin Shi, Stefano Ermon, *Sliced Score Matching: A Scalable Approach to Density and Score Estimation*, UAI 2019; PMLR 115:574–584. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v115/song20a.html>. The Hutchinson-trick reformulation that made score matching viable on images.
- Yang Song, Stefano Ermon, *Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution*, NeurIPS 2019; arXiv:1907.05600. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600>. Noise-conditional score networks; the first strong image-generation results from score matching and the paper that bridged it to diffusion.
- Yang Song, Diederik P. Kingma, *How to Train Your Energy-Based Models*, arXiv:2101.03288 (2021). <https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03288>. A short survey tying score matching to MCMC-based maximum likelihood and to noise-contrastive estimation; a good map of the landscape before you commit to one.
